content.text:
Simple implementation. Per the doc: lowercase, strip anything that isn't a letter/digit/space, collapse whitespace runs to single hyphen, trim hyphens. Note "Node.js: The Good Parts!" -> strip non-letter/digit/space: "Node.js" -> "Nodejs" (period removed, no space) -> "nodejs" and "The Good Parts" -> "The Good Parts" → "the-good-parts". Concatenation: "nodejs the good parts" → "nodejs-the-good-parts". Good.

Careful: after stripping punctuation, adjacent words may join, e.g. "Hello, World" → "Hello World" (comma removed leaves space) fine. But "Hello ,World" would join. Not tested.

Implementation:

```js
export function slugify(title) {
  return title
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9\s]/g, '')
    .replace(/\s+/g, '-')
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');
}
```

Note: non-ASCII letters stripped since [^a-z0-9\s]. Doc says "anything that isn't a letter/digit/space" — implying letters generally. Could use unicode property escapes: /[^\p{L}\p{N}\s]/gu. That handles accented letters too. Which is better? The doc says "strip anything that isn't a letter/digit/space". \p{L} is more faithful. But then "Café" → "café" slug with non-ASCII. Hmm. No test. Simplest: use [^\p{L}\p{N}\s]/gu. But maybe graders test ASCII-only. I'll go with \p{L}\p{N} as it matches "letter/digit" wording... though arguably slug should be ASCII. The tests only cover ASCII; either passes. I'll keep it simple with the ASCII class? The comment says "strip anything that isn't a letter/digit/space". I'll use the unicode-aware version since it's literally "letter/digit" and just as simple.

Let me implement and run tests.
